title: ‘Sweet Magnolias’ Creator Reacts to Netflix Cancellation: ‘I Hope Serenity Will Always Have a Place in Your Heart’
description: Following the news that “Sweet Magnolias” has been canceled at Netflix, creator and showrunner Sheryl J. Anderson is looking back on the romantic dr
body:
Following the news that “Sweet Magnolias” has been canceled at Netflix, creator and showrunner Sheryl J. Anderson is looking back on the romantic drama’s 5 Season run.

	“Living in Serenity for five seasons has been a privilege and a blessing,” Anderson shared in the caption of an Instagram post Saturday. “The people I’ve met and worked with — our incredible writers, cast, crew, executives, and producers — have touched my heart and changed my life.”
	

	She continued: “And our fans have been amazing in their passion for our characters. Thank you all. Though our journey has sadly come to an end, I hope Serenity will always have a place in your heart. Keep pouring it out!”


	The Netflix show first premiered on the platform in May 2020, and starred JoAnna Garcia Swisher, Brooke Elliott and Heather Headley. Originally adapted from the book series by New York Times best-selling author Sherryl Woods, the streamer announced that the show continuously ranked among Netflix’s Global Top 10 in over 60 countries after announcing its return for a fifth season in 2025.

	The “comfort drama,” as described by Netflix, followed the lifelong friendship between Maddie (Swisher), Dana Sue (Elliott), and Helen (Headley) “as they juggle relationships, family and careers in the charming small town of Serenity, S.C.”

	Though “Sweet Magnolias” may be coming to an end, Netflix announced that Swisher and Anderson would be teaming for a new drama series titled “Ladies of the House.”

	Variety previously reported that Anderson will serve as showrunner, with Swisher potentially starring and executive producing with Kate Gordon under their Rolling Clover banner, alongside executive producers at Black Label Media.
	

	The logline reads, “When the charismatic owner of a winery dies unexpectedly, his wife and two adult daughters must battle through their issues with each other in order to confront challenges with the business, their extended family, and the men in their lives. Good friends and good wine will aid in the journey to hang on to the winery, but what matters most is that they find a way to hang on to each other.”

schema.headline: ‘Sweet Magnolias’ Creator Reacts to Netflix Cancellation: ‘I Hope Serenity Will Always Have a Place in Your Heart’

title: Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Were Clowned for Buying the Staten Island Ferry. They Just Proved Everyone Wrong.
description:
“There’s an epidemic affecting our nation’s young people. The epidemic is fear.”

	As I scrolled through Instagram on my ride downtown to the Snappl
body:
“There’s an epidemic affecting our nation’s young people. The epidemic is fear.”

	As I scrolled through Instagram on my ride downtown to the Snapple Island Ferry Comedy Show, a reel from The Free Press popped up. Professor Arthur Brooks was making the case that “Gen Z is perhaps the most risk-averse generation in history.”

	Now, I’m no psychologist. I’m a social media editor. And I theorize that some of that fear Brooks describes comes from our overexposure to a digital world that, seemingly, has all the answers. And when someone makes a decision outside the purview of algorithmic logic — like buying an abandoned ferry for $280,000 at a city auction — they are at the mercy of, well, being completely clowned.
	

	That’s exactly what the news cycle did to Pete Davidson and Colin Jost after they joined a group of investors to buy the decommissioned John F. Kennedy in 2022. Built in 1965, the JFK was the oldest ferry in the Staten Island fleet when it was retired last August due to mechanical failures. Davidson and Jost intended to transform the vessel into a floating entertainment venue.“Davidson, who’s no longer with SNL, might need to call his agent to book those gigs — turning the 57-year-old ship into a nightspot is likely to cost millions,” The New York Daily News reported. The headline read: “Retired NY Ferry Bought by Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Is Full of Asbestos, Roaches, Say Ex-Crew Members.”

	The social media hate laid on thick, too: “Have you heard of the hottest club in the city?” one person tweeted (per the LA Times). “It’s called ‘Tetanus’ and it’s located in the rusted belly of a decommissioned Staten Island Ferry. You’ll dance the night away while also always being just moments away from drowning.”

	Years had passed without hearing about the ferry until I got an unexpected email in my inbox: “EMBARGOED: Invite to NYC’s Most Unexpected Comedy Club From Pete Davidson and Colin Jost.”
	

	As it turned out, the “SNL” comedians partnered with Snapple to give New Yorkers an “unexpectedly refreshing break from the daily grind,” transforming their vessel into the Snapple Staten Island Ferry for a free, one-night-only floating comedy show.

	Could the comedians have listed tickets for $200 a pop and still packed the ferry? Undoubtedly. Instead, they dropped a limited batch of free tickets at 3 p.m. each day (Sept. 3-8). The resulting buzz and scramble among young New Yorkers to secure tickets (not totally unlike the IMAX 70mm frenzy surrounding “The Odyssey”) was much more valuable than the low six figures a sold-out show might have grossed at the door.Those lucky enough to make it aboard became a test audience for two brand comebacks, each fiercely looking to win over a younger generation before betting on a much bigger, more calculated swing.

	The first is Snapple, which started phasing out its signature glass bottles in 2017, replacing them with plastic (the transition was complete by 2021). The company justified the brand’s “massive makeover” as a decision made “with the evolution of sustainability in mind.” The operational savings from slashing the cost of manufacturing a bottle to roughly a third of what it once was probably looked pretty savory to the big-wig execs at Keurig Dr Pepper. Consumers weren’t as quenched.



	

					Sean K Fitzpatrick
	



	Snapple eventually budged in the fall of 2025, launching a limited glass-bottle revival at select bodegas and retailers across New York, citing a “demand for nostalgia from an OVERWHELMING number of consumers.” The brand has yet to commit to a wider or permanent return, but it was clearly testing the waters with this major brand activation.

	Hosting Snapple’s revival party was Davidson and Jost’s own comeback project to replenish the New York comedy scene, taking the form of a floating, popsicle-orange vessel. They once played the purchase off as a joke on “SNL,” with Jost quipping, “We thought the whole thing through” (sarcasm implied). But four years later, this one-night-only comedy show offered them a real opportunity to float their idea.


	The main room was packed. Because the ferry, naturally, didn’t have one big corridor, an overflow room projected a live feed of the main stage (shaped like a blocky ‘T’).

	“You’re media, right?” an event coordinator asked me. “Yes!” I had zoned out. “Then we better put you up here.” She whisked me straight to the front and pointed at two young women, who immediately jolted to their feet and shuffled toward the far end of the bench running parallel to the stage.“I, uh, I’m sorry I took your seats,” I told the two women as I sidestepped past them. They glanced at each other and giggled. “It’s okay,” one of them said. “Trust me.”
	

	It took me a couple of minutes to figure out what she meant. Then I pulled out my phone to take a picture of the stage: a black barstool, a (glass!) Peach Tea Snapple and a mic stand. I wasn’t just in the front row. I was in the hot seat. The very hot seat, directly under the mic stand. Stage lights beamed down on me, and the ferry cabin itself was extremely muggy. (I guess in Davidson and Jost’s master plan, A/C hit the cutting room floor.)

	The room skewed younger millennials and older Gen Z. Most toward the front looked like (or probably were) influencers who’ll look good on camera. Usually, I’ll recognize at least a few media friends in a crowd like this. Not here. I tried making friendly banter with the dude sitting next to me. He was cordial, but his energy read: Nope.

	At nine o’clock sharp, the lights went dark. Davidson and Jost emerged from beneath the neon Snapple Island Ferry sign to rapturous applause. This would be the first and last time we’d see the two co-hosts all night.

	I’ve encountered Davidson and Jost in the wild before, but this tight vantage point popped any illusion of celebrity. Picture sitting in the front row of a movie theater.

	“This is something we’ve wanted to do for like five years, so thank you guys for coming out,” Davidson opened. “And thank you to our sponsor, Snapple.” After holding a beat for the applause, Davidson exclaimed, “The glass is back, baby!”

	Jost added: “I also feel like we should acknowledge our former sponsor: my accountant’s suicide note.” He smirked. “Snapple asked me to say this.”

	They then turned to the first of three lingering storylines from the news cycle they clearly wanted to address. First, the aforementioned clowning.“The amount of shit that people have talked,” Davidson said. “Well, suck it!”

	“Everyone feeling hot and nauseous? That’s a good feeling,” Jost asked the crowd before moving on to news topic numero dos. “Obviously we’ll get going soon. We’re gonna stop at the Strait of Hormuz.” But when Jost looked over at Davidson to tee up the next punchline, it became clear the geopolitical reference sailed right over his head.

	“I like how you thought I would know what that is,” Davidson quipped back. He glanced down at the shot clock. 8:17 remaining. The sweat was palpable.

	“I love that this is our body language,” Davidson said, leaning into their candid awkwardness as he and Jost stood marooned on opposite ends of the oversized T-shaped stage. “It’s truly like we’re waiting for someone to start a fight.”
	

	Laughing along with the crowd, Jost admitted, “We don’t know exactly what to do.” The audience roared. That unvarnished honesty, the willingness to take themselves down a notch, clearly resonated with the audience of young people accustomed to spending hours each day swiping through content engineered to mask imperfection.

	“We have an incredible show. There are so many great comedians here,” Jost said. “Macklemore is here tonight.” The crowd erupted. Jost stalled on a few uhs, his eyes scanning the room as he debated whether it was worth taking the joke any further.

	Davidson took advantage of the moment. “You wanted to make a stance tonight, right?” he poked. “Colin was talking mad shit backstage, dude. He was like, ‘Macklemore doesn’t have shit on what I’m about to say.’”

	Red in the face, Jost quickly rowed back to safer waters. “So, in other news…” From there, the remainder of their opener centered on Davidson’s recent concussion. But the lineup of fierce rising comics (with considerably less to lose) didn’t shy away from the insecurities and taboos their Gen Z audience might be too anxious to confront.

	Matt Richards, who served as emcee for the night (effectively filling the role many of us presumed Davidson and Jost would play), set the tone for the night by chugging an entire Snapple in one go and then telling a story of how he tried to suck his own penis as a teenager. “Happy to say it didn’t work out,” Richards said. “If it did, I wouldn’t be here.” In an alternate timeline, he’d “live under a bridge and suck my own dick all day.”

	As the crowd observed Richards, he gauged their reactions, taking the temperature of how far he could push them. The other comics were about to dive into some risqué material — he was just warming them up.

	Richards wiped a bulk of sweat from his forehead. The humidity was becoming hard to ignore. Playfully, he advised Davidson and Jost to sort out the A/C situation before the next show. That’s what I was thinking.


	When Chris Rock sat down with Variety’s Selome Hailu for his first in-depth interview since “The Slap,” he recalled “dying a death” during a stand-up set in Oakland in ’96. He was workshopping his controversial “Black People Versus N—s” bit, which would eventually appear in his landmark HBO special “Bring the Pain” that helped catapult Rock into rock-star comic status.

	“People wanted to fight because I didn’t have it right yet,” Rock explained in his cover story interview. “You gotta go over the line to find the line. That’s what people don’t understand. When a comedian gets in trouble for saying something at the club, it’s like, ‘Dude, that’s what the club’s for.’”

	Overcoming the fear of vulnerability, on both sides of the stage, is what makes the club special. A physical vessel where smartphones, despite the event’s plea for ample social coverage, were repeatedly told to stay tucked away.
	

	At one point, a Staten Island photographer named Sean lowered his camera to snap a portrait on his phone of “Impractical Jokers” star Sal Vulcano mid-set. Vulcano immediately stopped. “No cellphones, sir,” he said. “It’s right up in my face.” Sean held up his DSLR, cutting Vulcano’s budding rant short.

	“This guy’s just like- oh, you work here?” Vulcano said, his tone instantly changing. “Okay, you’re not fired. You’re great. I love you.”

	Even an Impractical Joker, after hundreds of public challenges and punishments designed to push the limits of embarrassment, could still tense up when a cellphone camera caught him experimenting with a new bit. “That was the ending,” he told the crowd after telling a story about buying health insurance for his newborn. “I thought that would get a bigger laugh.”

	The crowd loved it. He was hyper-fixated on grading his performance.

	Perhaps that’s why crowd work is so effective. Is there any other setting better designed to experience a flash of public humiliation?“I like this guy,” Richards said, pointing at me. “You look like a Disney villain.”

	“Gaston!” He belted out a Disney song. 

	Caitlin Peluffo stormed the stage with material in the — let’s call it — advanced workshopping stages. After boldly announcing to the crowd that she was “dropping eggs,” she turned to ask if I knew what ovulating was.

	I responded with a sarcastic “Ehh!” and bobbed my head. “Go figure,” she said. “I wouldn’t expect anything less from a man wearing khakis.”

	After another minute or two of hyper-sexual jokes, she circled back to me.

	“Do you like pussy?”
	

	The camera whipped in my direction.

	I froze. Then hit her with the same ambiguous emote.

	Why did I just do that? I literally-

	“You’re really wishy-washy on the answer, sir.”

	“You gotta leave a little mystery.”

	“Leave a little mystery?”

	Gulp.

	“Those pants aren’t leaving any mystery, I’ll tell you that,” she fired back. “You’re not circumcised, I can tell.” The crowd woo-ed. “That’s okay. I like me a full-body boy,” she continued. “I’m not an easy cum. You better crack your knuckles.”

	I cracked my knuckles on both hands. She smiled. Peluffo got what she needed from me. Mercifully, she moved on to her next victim.

	“Are you a tough cum or an easy cum?” she asked an attractive, reserved young woman. “Which one are you?” I had never seen a face more red in my entire life. “ANSWER THE FUCKING QUESTION!”

	“I’m easy!” she finally blurted out.

	“Fuck!” Peluffo shot back. “You’re probably cumming right now.”


	On the way out, ferry workers dressed in sailor uniforms were handing departing guests free Snapple. I grabbed a glass peach tea and popped a squat on the pier. It really does taste better.

	As I sat there taking in the night, the sound of clinking glass got louder and louder. Sure enough, I spotted a small procession bolting away from the boat with entire cases of Snapple.

	I walked over and asked a few of the workers why they were giving them away. A woman with a dyed-blonde bob leaned toward me, lowering her voice.

	“Please, take one now and leave before anyone sees you,” she said. “We need to get rid of all of these before the end of the night.”



	

					Sean K Fitzpatrick

schema.headline: Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Were Clowned for Buying the Staten Island Ferry. They Just Proved Everyone Wrong.

title: Henry Winkler Says His Name Was Cut From ‘Scream’ Poster Because ‘You Were the Fonz’ and It Would ‘Knock the Balance of Horror Off’
description:
Finding out his name wouldn’t be used on the “Scream” poster wasn’t one of Henry Winkler’s happier days.

	The “Happy Days” star played Principal Ar
body:
Finding out his name wouldn’t be used on the “Scream” poster wasn’t one of Henry Winkler’s happier days.

	The “Happy Days” star played Principal Arthur Himbry in the original “Scream” film, which went on to become one of the most successful horror franchises. But despite his character’s entrance receiving applause during screen tests for the 1996 movie, Winkler revealed the studio refused to put his name on the poster.
	

	“The studio comes to me and says, ‘We can’t put your name on the film. We cannot put you anywhere near the poster,’” Winkler said in an interview for “In Depth With Graham Besinger.” When he asked why, the studio said, “Well, you were the Fonz, and you will knock the balance of horror off if we let them know you’re in it.”


	Although it left him feeling “insulted,” the actor didn’t overtly protest the studio’s decision. 

	“I said, ‘OK. What can I do?’ I went home upset,” the actor said. “I was bewildered a little bit.”

	He later learned the same people who had informed him his name wouldn’t be used on the poster were also the ones who asked him if he would do press for the film’s release. Winkler ultimately agreed, noting he obliged for himself, director Wes Craven and the movie as a whole.

	Now, looking back 30 years later, Winkler said the experience taught him to navigate the unknown.

	“That’s the lesson. You just show up,” he said, also pointing out that “you have no idea what’s going to happen, but that’s out of your control.”

	“Scream” also starred Neve Campbell, Courteney Cox, David Arquette, Drew Barrymore and Matthew Lillard. The franchise’s latest film, “Scream 7,” became the highest-grossing installment with $176.9 million.

schema.headline: Henry Winkler Says His Name Was Cut From ‘Scream’ Poster Because ‘You Were the Fonz’ and It Would ‘Knock the Balance of Horror Off’

title: ‘The Smell of Apples’ Review: A Sun-Soaked but Chilling Child’s-Eye View of Apartheid-Era Privilege and Denial
description: Every surface period detail is present and correct to an eerie degree in “The Smell of Apples“: the gawkily short seasonal school uniforms, the icki
body:
Every surface period detail is present and correct to an eerie degree in “The Smell of Apples“: the gawkily short seasonal school uniforms, the ickily patterned kitchen tiles, the garden chairs like steel satellite dishes, the orange-and-brown daisy print that anyone of a certain age will recognize from sundry towels, mattresses and beach umbrellas. Production designer Birrie Le Roux has crafted a pristine one-way time capsule to mid-1970s white South Africa; DP Lennert Hillege shoots it to softly lit, summer-burnt perfection. But there’s not a whisper of nostalgia to “The Smell of Apples,” director John Trengove‘s slowly, then suddenly, piercing evocation of affluent Afrikaner family life in that era, and the litany of egregious abuses and inequalities propping it up. It’s told through the eyes of a naïve 11-year-old boy, but there’s no halo to his innocence — just a growing awareness of how much he doesn’t know, none of it good.
	

	Drawn from a well-regarded 1993 novel by Mark Behr that has become a popular set text in South African schools and universities, “The Smell of Apples” joins other recent literary adaptations like Oliver Hermanus’ “Moffie” and Embeth Davidtz’s “Don’t Let’s Go to the Dogs Tonight” in articulating the experiences of white people living inside an Apartheid bubble just on the verge of bursting. It’s a discomfiting and not especially fashionable point of focus; as in those films, we get only deliberately glancing, peripheral views of the black majority, their anguish never openly voiced. But these glaring blind spots, however hard to watch, are the point. “The Smell of Apples” intelligently demonstrates the effortful compartmentalization and denial that kept a system of white supremacy in place.
	

	It’s a successful homecoming for Trengove, the Johannesburger who made a searing feature debut with the Sundance prizewinner “The Wound,” about ritual initiation and repressed sexuality in the traditional Xhosa community, before heading to the U.S. for his Jesse Eisenberg-starring follow-up “Manodrome,” a commendably ambitious but stifled manosphere study. “The Smell of Apples” resumes those films’ preoccupation with toxic masculine influence across generations, as well as their queer framing — though in a surprising departure from the novel, the latter is restricted to subtextual intimations.

	Indeed, Trengove and co-writer Christopher Ciancimino’s impressively minimalist adaptation strips away much of Behr’s structural foreshadowing and underlining, including the novel’s flash-forwards to the child protagonist’s adult military service in the South African Border War. As it is, there’s an ample sense on screen of the plunging darkness toward which the country is headed, before any kind of dawn can establish itself, while it’s impossible not to feel the military’s past, present and future stranglehold on young Marnus Erasmus (Dawian van der Westhuizen, a real talent) at every turn. The only son of Johan (Hilton Pelser), the country’s youngest Army general, Marnus has a world of macho Afrikaner ideology to live up to, but already the boy, timid and fair and small for his age, suspects he might be a disappointment.

	Johan generally treats Marnus with bluff good humor, though you can see the anxious scrutiny with which he sizes his son up — and when that worry gets the better of him, it emerges violently. Marnus’ best friend Frikkie (Wian Carstens) is a strapping, bullish lad, and when he’s over, which is often, Johan tends to treat him like another, stronger son — Marnus may feel a little frozen out by their bond, but he’s too shy and stoic to say so. “A father looks at his sons and sees his own shortcomings,” says enigmatic houseguest Mr. Smith (Alejandro Goic) to Marnus, and that’s no great comfort. Nor is Mr. Smith himself: a Chilean Army general, fresh from his role in the Pinochet coup, with whom Johan is covertly consulting about matters beyond Marnus’ understanding. 

	His homemaker mother Leonor (a superb Maude Sandham) and his 17-year-old sister Ilse (Karoline Watson) complete the immaculate family portrait, but there’s unrest there too. Ilse, a high-flyer at her conservative Afrikaans high school, is gradually catching wise to her father’s entitlement and cruelty, and to the injustices of the Apartheid government; Leonor puts on a brave face as she projects exactly the image her husband needs her to, but is unnerved by the barbed critiques of her liberal sister Karla (Inge Beckmann), who, by Johan’s decree, is not welcome in the family’s rambling, lushly landscaped Cape Town home. 
	

	The person who keeps that home shipshape, of course, is not Leonor but Doreen (Celeste Matthews Wannenburgh), the family’s black live-in maid — a longtime fixture whom Marnus takes too much for granted to fully realize his emotional attachment to her. (Her routine pet name for him is kleinbaas, which translates as “little boss,” and it’s said with weary affection but no irony.) The family, of course, would say Doreen is a valued part of the household, though her place in it is made quite clear when her orphaned teenage grandson Neville (Courtlin Baron) arrives to stay in her servants’ quarters, and is made most unwelcome by the master of the house. An exquisitely composed shot of Doreen, slumped in the kitchen half-light as she eavesdrops on the family’s dining-room discussion of Neville’s fate, encapsulates a world of upstairs-downstairs, black-white hierarchies.

	Over a tight five-day timeline — as Marnus and Ilse finish school ahead of the December holidays, and the family prepares for their summer vacation — these various tensions impact one another in tacit but perhaps terminal ways. Some are mere faultlines, others crack into unavoidable conflicts, though they collectively unmask the ugly face of authority in South Africa in ways even the young, fanciful Marnus can’t blithely look past. The sins of the father are ultimately presented in a literal, stomach-churning slideshow that haphazardly alternates benign family snaps with gleeful photographic evidence of Johan’s war crimes. 

	It’s a queasy climactic setpiece — one that tests, in particular, the brittle wifely composure so precisely enacted by Sandham — though matters here don’t come quite as tidily to a head as they do in Behr’s novel, which culminated in a shocking act of transgression that you sense may be afoot in the film, though it’s never confirmed. “The Smell of Apples” isn’t less powerful for this elision: It works toward a state of forced family stability, everyone that bit more frightened and mistrusting of each other, but held stiffly in place by their own privilege and power. You can feel Trengove’s film, so beautifully crafted and impeccably paced, sometimes bristling against its own fine construction — anticipating the destruction of this walled-off, deeply ugly idyll.

schema.headline: ‘The Smell of Apples’ Review: A Sun-Soaked but Chilling Child’s-Eye View of Apartheid-Era Privilege and Denial

	After Isl
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	After Islam Makhachev defended his welterweight title against Ian Machado Garry during UFC 330 in August, the Ultimate Fighting Championship travels from Philadelphia to Los Angeles for UFC 331. For the main event, Burmese fighter Joshua Van (17-2-0) defends his flyweight title belt against Brazilian Alexandre Pantoja (30-6-0) in a marquee match. It’s scheduled for five rounds.

	On Saturday, Sept. 19, UFC 331: Van vs. Pantoja takes place at Crypto.com Arena in L.A., California. The event starts at 5 p.m. ET/2 p.m. PT, while the main card is set to begin at 9 p.m. ET/6 p.m. PT.


	In late 2025, Joshua Van defeated Alexandre Pantoja in 26 seconds to win the UFC Flyweight Championship belt during UFC 323. Van has reigned as champion for nearly a year, while Pantoja worked to get back into the octagon to reclaim the title. However, Van is the odds on favorite to defend his belt, but Pantoja isn’t going to make it easy for him. Pantoja is healthy and eager to win back the crown.

	And since UFC 331 is a high profile event in L.A., it’s likely the MMA event may feature a few of celebrities in attendance, such as Shane Gillis, Anthony Kiedis, Chris Pratt, Shaquille O’Neal and others.

	If you’re interested in attending, yourself, last-minute tickets are still available for UFC 331 in L.A. Retailers, like Ticketmaster, StubHub, Vivid Seats, SeatGeek, TicketNetwork, Gametime and others, all have tickets for sale for Crypto.com Arena.

	The event is available to livestream on Paramount+. UFC 331 is not a pay-per-view (PPV) livestream. You just need access to Paramount+ to watch it live.


		

						
			
	

					Paramount+
	
					
		

					Paramount+		

	
		Prices start at $8.99/month	
		
	

	For new subscribers, UFC 331 starts at $8.99/month for the Paramount+ Essential plan for access to all UFC events (included numbered and fight night events).

	Aside from streaming access to Paramount+ to watch UFC, you can take advantage of everything Walmart+ has to offer with perks such as free and fast delivery; fuel discounts at Walmart, Sam’s Club, Exxon, Mobil and Murphy stations; Burger King deals; additional savings with early access deals and many other perks. Learn more about what Walmart+ can offer you here.

	No matter which Paramount+ plan you pick, you’ll have access to UFC 331 at no additional cost.

title: Singer Aaron Rowe Defends Ed Sheeran After Dropping Out of Tour: ‘It Was Human F—ing Error’
description: Aaron Rowe, who was one of the opening acts on Ed Sheeran’s tour before pulling out after Macklemore’s dismissal over his support for Palestine, has
body:
Aaron Rowe, who was one of the opening acts on Ed Sheeran’s tour before pulling out after Macklemore’s dismissal over his support for Palestine, has now issued an impassioned defense of the singer.

	“I think you are all focusing on the wrong person here. All I keep hearing is Ed Sheeran this, Ed Sheeran that. When you really should be focusing on the likes of Robert Kraft. You really should be focusing on the Zionist lobbies that are trying to silence the voices of people who are shouting about genocide, the genocide that is happening in Palestine right now by Israel,” said Rowe in a video posted to his Instagram account Friday.
	

	He continued: “Look, I know Ed’s statement could have been a lot better, and I do think that Macklemore shouldn’t have been pulled off the tour. I fully believe it was panic station over there, and they rushed the decision because they didn’t know what to fucking do because they were getting it from all angles. That’s a mistake… I haven’t had a chance to fucking talk to Ed too much, but I fully believe he knows that was a mistake.”


	Rowe went on to point out that most of the artists in Sheeran’s opening lineup support Palestine. “Look who’s on the fucking lineup, yeah? Beoga, the most pro-Palestine group out there…. fully pro-Palestine, fucking Macklemore. Need I say more? Me, everyone knows my fucking stance on Palestine. Like, if Ed Sheeran was a fucking Zionist, why would he have all these fucking people on the fucking tour? It was human fucking error.”

	The Irish singer-songwriter’s video comes as Sheeran continues to receive backlash for Macklemore’s removal from the tour. In addition to Rowe, Finneas, another opener, also dropped out of the tour. When Rowe dropped out, he acknowledged that Sheeran had “changed my life,” a point he honed in on again in this video.
	

	“I know Ed Sheeran has done so much for so many fucking people, including artists like me, who he’s literally changed their entire lives. All he has inside of him is kindness. That is who Ed Sheeran is. And yes, like every other human being, he makes fucking mistakes.”

	Rowe concluded: “You should be using this opportunity to plaster Robert Kraft’s face everywhere. Someone who tried to shut down free speech. Someone who tried to silence the voices of people who are shouting about genocide. That’s what you should be using your energy on, not fucking Ed Sheeran, for fuck’s sake.”

schema.headline: Singer Aaron Rowe Defends Ed Sheeran After Dropping Out of Tour: ‘It Was Human F—ing Error’

title: Gavin Newsom Signs Bill Creating $10 Million Post-Production Tax Credit
description: Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed a measure to create a $10 million tax credit meant to stem the tide of post-production jobs to other states and oversea
body:
Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed a measure to create a $10 million tax credit meant to stem the tide of post-production jobs to other states and overseas.

	The bill, AB 2319, passed the state Assembly and Senate last month by wide margins. Supporters, including the Motion Picture Editors Guild, had pushed for a credit that would be tenfold larger — $100 million — but see the more modest allocation as a positive first step.


	Scott George, the guild’s national executive director, called the signing a “historic day” and said the credit will ensure that “even projects shooting outside of our state can come back to California to employ Editors Guild members in post-production.”
	

	The California Post Alliance, a coalition of post-production facilities, also campaigned strongly for the bill. Supporters have noted that many countries — including the U.K., Canada, Australia and Spain — have standalone tax incentives for post-production, as do several other U.S. states, including New York, New Mexico and New Jersey.

	California, meanwhile, increased its film and TV tax credit to $750 million last year. That credit covers post-production costs, but only if 75% of the project’s overall budget is spent in California. The new credit would allow productions to film elsewhere but still get a subsidy for in-state editing and VFX work.

	One of the challenges in getting the bill passed is that the VFX industry remains largely non-union, and state lawmakers are typically unwilling to subsidize jobs that could undercut union labor. The bill was amended in May to require that 85% of the funding go to jobs with union-level wages and benefits.
	

	Assemblyman Nick Schultz, D-Burbank, led the effort in the Legislature. According to his office, the post-production industry employs about 12,000 people in the state, but has lost 1,874 jobs over the last 20 years.

	“This is a big victory in our fight to save California’s entertainment industry, and we’re just getting started,” Schultz said.

	Newsom also signed SB 186, which addresses the film industry’s concerns about the state’s $5 million cap on corporate tax credits. The measure exempts independent films from the cap, and allows studios to accelerate the payback period on refundable tax credits from five years to two years. The measure also extends the expiration date on old, non-refundable tax credits from nine years to 15 years.

	The industry had pushed for a complete exemption for film tax credits from the cap, but did not get that.

schema.headline: Gavin Newsom Signs Bill Creating $10 Million Post-Production Tax Credit

title: Elizabeth Warren Says it Would be a ‘Massive Mistake’ for Rob Bonta to Settle Lawsuit With Paramount as Trump Bans CNN from White House: ‘This Is a Dangerous Merger’
description:
Sep 19, 2026 1:10pm PT	
	

	
		Elizabeth Warren Says it Would be a ‘Massive Mistake’ for Rob Bonta to Settle Lawsuit With Paramount as
body:
Sep 19, 2026 1:10pm PT	
	

	
		Elizabeth Warren Says it Would be a ‘Massive Mistake’ for Rob Bonta to Settle Lawsuit With Paramount as Trump Bans CNN from White House: ‘This Is a Dangerous Merger’
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Getty
	

		
	
				
	Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts on Saturday morning issued a warning that President Donald Trump’s recent banning of CNN from the White House is a sign of things to come if Paramount Skydance settles with the states and is allowed to merge with Warner Bros.

	“As Trump tries to ban CNN from the White House, it would be a massive mistake to cave on the Paramount merger,” Warren wrote on Facebook. “The last thing we need is another Trump-controlled media conglomerate abusing its power to stomp out competition. This is a dangerous merger.”
	

	Trump announced on Friday that he was banning CNN, along with MS NOW and Politico, from the White House because of their “fake news” reporting. The Trump administration followed through on that promise Saturday morning, denying White House access to several staffers from the outlets.


	CNN said in a statement: “Early today, CNN journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. CNN’s mission to report on the U.S. government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism. We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right.”

	On the Paramount-Warner Bros. front, David Ellison’s $111 billion deal is at a standstill thanks to a lawsuit from California attorney general Rob Bonta and 11 other state AGs. The Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing anonymous sources, that the Paramount Skydance camp is in “advanced talks” with Bonta and the states to settle the suit. 


	
		More from Variety

title: Melissa Barrera Says Support for Macklemore After He Was Dropped from Ed Sheeran’s Tour Is ‘Beautiful’ and ‘I Didn’t Get That’ After Being Fired From ‘Scream’
description: Melissa Barrera, who was fired from the “Scream” franchise due to social media posts criticizing Israel amid the war in Gaza in 2023, is voicing her
body:
Melissa Barrera, who was fired from the “Scream” franchise due to social media posts criticizing Israel amid the war in Gaza in 2023, is voicing her respect for the musicians who have dropped out of Ed Sheeran’s tour following Macklemore’s dismissal over his support for Palestine.

	“It was so beautiful to see Finneas and the band and all the opening acts pulling out in support of Macklemore,” the actress said (via AP). “It made me emotional. You know, I didn’t get that when it happened to me. I didn’t have any of that happen. It was too soon. People were too scared. But it’s good to see that almost three years later, at least things have changed.”
	

	Macklemore was removed from Ed Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour after delivering a political speech and saying “Free Palestine” while onstage at the Sept. 4 concert at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The singer told the audience he wanted people in Gaza and the occupied West Bank to know they had not been forgotten. He was then dropped from the tour days later on Sep. 14.


	In the time since, openers including Finneas and Aaron Rowe have pulled out of the tour, citing their support for the “Thrift Shop” singer. 

	When Barrera was fired by “Scream” franchise producer Spyglass, the company said it had “zero tolerance for antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form, including false references to genocide, ethnic cleansing, Holocaust distortion or anything that flagrantly crosses the line into hate speech.” She had starred in 2022’s “Scream” and that year’s “Scream VI.” 
	

	At the time, Barrera’s fellow “Scream” cast members remained largely mum on her firing. While both Jenna Ortega and director Christopher Landon dropped out of “Scream 7,” released earlier this year, only recently did co-star Matthew Lillard say he feels “ashamed” for starring in the 2026 installment in the horror franchise.

	Barrera continued: “When someone is attacked, and there are people behind being like, ‘We’re not gonna allow this,’ and the more that happens, the less that the people in power are going to try to censor it because eventually it’s not gonna work. I can’t help but wonder what would have happened if Ed Sheeran had been like, ‘No,’ and called the bluff. I mean, it’s possible that he still would have had his shows canceled, but I bet you that he could have rebooked those shows in other venues just as easily, and people would have rallied behind him.”

	“I wish that the people that have power understood the power that they have,” she concluded. “I think that the problem is that there’s a lot of people that actually have a lot of power. They think they don’t, and they’re operating out of fear, and it’s just a shame because, you know, we just saw what happened—the support that rallied behind Macklemore—and I think that’s a big step. I think that what we’re seeing, what we’re witnessing, is going to inspire real change, and I’m very hopeful about that.”

schema.headline: Melissa Barrera Says Support for Macklemore After He Was Dropped from Ed Sheeran’s Tour Is ‘Beautiful’ and ‘I Didn’t Get That’ After Being Fired From ‘Scream’

            UMass Dartmouth running back Marvins Antoine has been fatally stabbed after an attack at a fast-food parking lot ... he was only 18 years old.
      
    
            The stabbing -- which saw Marvins suffering wounds to his chest -- took place at a Wendy's parking lot in Providence early Saturday morning ... WJAR initially reported.
      
    
            Marvin was declared dead upon arrival after being brought to a nearby hospital ... WPRI reported.
      

            Meanwhile, one of Marvin's 19-year-old teammates was treated for "non-life-threatening injuries" ... according to WJAR.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The two reportedly had gone to a local nightlife venue across the street from the Wendy's on Friday with other members of the team.
      
    
            Apparently, the club became overcrowded, and they closed their doors to new arrivals ... Providence Police Major David Lapatin said, according to WPRI. It was then that the fatal fight broke out.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A suspect is currently in custody ... according to the UMass Dartmouth Police Department.
      
    
            UMass Dartmouth said in a statement ... "The entire UMass Dartmouth community mourns the loss of Marvins Antoine. We extend our thoughts and prayers to Marvins family and friends during this difficult time."

President Trump
                          I Will Create an A.I. Force!!!
body:
President Trump
                          I Will Create an A.I. Force!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 19, 2026
                            12:41 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            First there was Space Force ... now, President Donald Trump has announced that in order to monitor artificial intelligence, he will create -- you guessed it -- an A.I. Force.
      
    
            The prez took to Truth Social Saturday morning to claim that the growing concern about the nefarious capabilities of A.I. are simply part of a hoax ... this despite several members of the tech community direly sounding the alarm and sharing instances of A.I. going rogue.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He wrote ... "We will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth of this incredible industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"
      

            Having said that, Trump wrote that he'd be looking out for "BAD" instances of the technology acting out.
      
    
            The president added ... "For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.'"
      
    
            In the last two weeks, there's been a slew of disturbing revelations about the technology ... and some of what's gone down is downright eerie.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The U.S. military reportedly almost started a war with China based on a faulty intelligence report generated by A.I. ... and OpenAI just shared their discovery of 6 "unexpected or concerning" new incidents.
      
    
            Time will tell if Trump can get his A.I. Force to lift off in time ... before A.I. goes too far.
